passage: I'm Ganga, and I've always hummed when I'm calm. On the walk to the bus stop, a little tune from an old film would come out without me noticing, and my brother Farhan used to tease me that I sounded like a kettle. It made me happy. Then one evening at the crossing a man on a bike whistled at me, loud and long, and slowed down to look. My humming stopped. My stomach went cold. I stepped into a shop and waited. Afterwards I told Farhan, who went with me to report it at the college gate desk. They noted it down. I still hum, but I hum by the window where I feel safe.

qa.q: Where did the man on the bike whistle at Ganga?
qa.a: The man whistled at Ganga at the crossing.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when the humming stopped?
qa.a: Ganga was frightened and unsafe, shown by the cold stomach and stepping into a shop. The whistle was aimed at a person and felt like harassment, unlike the tune Ganga hums alone.

qa.q: What steps did Ganga take to stay safe?
qa.a: Ganga stepped into a shop, waited, told Farhan, Ganga's brother, and reported it at the college gate desk.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt on hearing about it?
qa.a: Farhan probably felt worried and protective, and going with Ganga to report it shows he took Ganga's feelings seriously.

grounding: Humming can bring calm or joy, but a whistle aimed at a person in public can be harassment, and the person may leave and report it.

passage: Note from Ms. Himani, hostel warden. On Thursday evening Pallavi came to the office, pale and quiet. She said a group of young men outside the gate had whistled and made kissing sounds at her on her way back from the library. She had walked faster and felt her hands shaking. I listened without interrupting and told her that this was not her fault and not acceptable. I noted the time and place with her permission, and we spoke about who could walk with her in the evenings. Pallavi wanted to report it, so I helped her fill in the complaint form with the college. I will check on her tomorrow.

qa.q: Where did the whistling happen?
qa.a: It happened outside the gate as Pallavi returned from the library.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she came to the office?
qa.a: Pallavi felt frightened and unsettled, with pale colour and shaking hands. The warden cannot know all she felt, but her quiet manner and her wish to report suggest she was upset.

qa.q: What did Himani do that supported Pallavi?
qa.a: Himani listened, said it was not Pallavi's fault, noted the time and place with permission, and helped fill in the complaint form.

qa.q: What might the warden have been concerned about while listening to Pallavi?
qa.a: The warden was likely concerned for Pallavi's safety, so the warden listened without interrupting, said it was not her fault and planned who could walk with her in the evenings.

grounding: Whistling and kissing sounds at a person in public is unwelcome harassment, and anyone targeted may report it and be supported.

passage:
Friday, 8 p.m.
I always hum on the walk home from the bus stop. Old film songs, badly. It's the one part of the day that's just mine.
Today, at the corner near the paan shop, a man on a scooter slowed down and gave a long whistle, looking right at me. Then another one. My humming stopped in my throat. I kept walking faster, didn't look at him. He laughed and rode off.
I called Bhupen from the next lane, because he'd told me to call anytime. He stayed on the phone till I reached my building. When I got home I told Mummy, and she said, "Beti, we'll tell the RWA secretary tomorrow and ask about the streetlight at that corner." She also saved the number for the women's helpline in my phone.
Funny how it's the same sound, whistling. When Bhupen whistles on the terrace, it's happy. That one wasn't.
— Nikita

qa.q: Where did the man on the scooter whistle at Nikita?
qa.a: At the corner near the paan shop.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when the man whistled?
qa.a: She felt scared and unsettled; her humming stopped in her throat and she walked faster without looking at him.

qa.q: What steps did Nikita and her mother take after the whistling?
qa.a: Nikita called Bhupen to stay on the phone, told Mummy, who planned to tell the RWA secretary and ask about the streetlight, and saved the helpline number.

qa.q: How is Bhupen's whistling different from the man's?
qa.a: Bhupen whistles on the terrace because he is happy; the man whistled at Nikita as a stranger on the street, which made her feel unsafe.

grounding: Shows humming and whistling as calm or joyful sounds, and a whistle aimed at a person in public as unwelcome harassment that she leaves and reports.

passage:
Preeti: saw you on the college gate video lol. you were whistling the whole song 😄
Ujjwal: haha it's my exam-over whistle. I'm always doing that
Preeti: it's cute when you do it at the canteen
Ujjwal: thanks. but can I ask you something weird
Preeti: go
Ujjwal: today Nikhil whistled at a girl crossing the road. like the long filmy one. she looked scared
Preeti: ugh. that's not whistling, that's harassment
Ujjwal: that's what I said. he said "it's just fun, relax"
Preeti: fun for who?
Ujjwal: exactly. I told him if he does it again I'm not walking with him. and I told the girl sorry and pointed her to the security guard at the gate
Preeti: did she go?
Ujjwal: yes. guard spoke to Nikhil too
Preeti: good. keep the canteen whistle. drop the Nikhil one 🙂

qa.q: What does Ujjwal call his whistling?
qa.a: His exam-over whistle.

qa.q: How did the girl crossing the road seem to feel when Nikhil whistled?
qa.a: She looked scared, which shows the whistle felt threatening to her, not fun.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that helped?
qa.a: Ujjwal told Nikhil it wasn't okay, refused to keep walking with Nikhil if it happened again, apologised to the girl and pointed her to the security guard.

qa.q: How does Preeti see the difference between the two kinds of whistle?
qa.a: Preeti sees Ujjwal's canteen whistle as cute and joyful, but a whistle aimed at a girl on the road as harassment.

grounding: Shows the difference between whistling for joy and whistling at a person in public, and a young adult recognising and responding to harassment.

passage: Tanvir always whistled while he worked the pump in his family's field near Barabanki; it kept the rhythm of the long afternoons. His friend Tushar whistled too, but differently. Every evening when the college bus dropped the girls from the next village at the crossing, Tushar leaned on his cycle and whistled long, loud notes at them, grinning. Tanvir used to laugh along. This evening he noticed one of the girls, Shabnam, walk faster, clutching her bag, eyes on the ground. Her friend pulled her closer. Tanvir's stomach tightened. "Stop it," he said to Tushar. "They're scared." "It's just a whistle, yaar." "Not to them." Tushar rolled his eyes. The next day, the girls' teacher came with the pradhan and spoke to both boys' fathers. Tushar sulked. Tanvir admitted he'd laughed along and said sorry. That evening he kept whistling at the pump, and nowhere near the crossing.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir whistle while he worked?
qa.a: At the pump in his family's field near Barabanki.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he saw Shabnam walk faster?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and guilty, his stomach tightening, as he realised the whistling was frightening the girls.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do once he saw it was wrong?
qa.a: He told Tushar to stop, and when the teacher and pradhan came, he admitted he had laughed along and apologised.

qa.q: How did Shabnam and her friend experience Tushar's whistling?
qa.a: They seemed scared, walking faster and pulling close, so for them it was harassment, not fun.

grounding: Shows whistling as calm work rhythm in one setting and as unwelcome harassment when aimed at girls in public, and recognising the difference.

passage: Leila always whistled on her walk to the bakery in Marseille, a tuneless little song that meant the morning was going well. Her friend Esther said it was like walking beside a kettle. On Saturday, waiting for the tram at Castellane, they heard a different whistle: two sharp notes aimed at Esther from a man leaning on a pillar. Then again, louder, with a "hey, beautiful." Esther pulled her jacket closed and stared hard at the timetable. Leila's own tune died in her throat. Same sound, she thought, but his wasn't a song. It was a hand on the shoulder nobody asked for. "Let's move," Leila said, and they walked to the far end of the platform, near the staff booth. Esther told the attendant what had happened. The attendant nodded, radioed security, and stayed beside them until the tram came. Leila didn't whistle again until they were off the tram.

qa.q: Where did Leila usually whistle?
qa.a: On her walk to the bakery.

qa.q: What was Leila feeling when her own tune died?
qa.a: Leila felt uneasy and angry on Esther's behalf, seeing that the same sound she used for joy had become an unwelcome intrusion.

qa.q: What did they do that helped?
qa.a: They moved away to the staff booth and reported it; the attendant radioed security and stayed with them until the tram came.

qa.q: What was it like for Esther when the man whistled?
qa.a: She likely felt uncomfortable and unsafe, pulling her jacket closed and staring at the timetable to shut out the attention.

grounding: It illustrates that whistling can express calm or joy, but whistling at a person in public can be harassment, and a targeted person may leave and report it.
